1. The Upper GI Tract and Types of Emesis

  • Upper GI tract = mouth/tongue, oropharynx, esophagus, stomach, and the first part of the small intestine (duodenum, including the ampulla of Vater, where the bile duct and pancreatic duct empty into the duodenum).
  • Symptoms of upper GI dysfunction: trouble with swallowing/feeding, often with emesis. Vomiting is one of the most common pediatric chief complaints.
Upper GI tract (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Emesis red flags: what the color or character tells you

EmesisSource / meaning
Bloody (bright red)Bleed from the esophagus or higher (e.g. swallowed blood from a nosebleed); possibly stomach if it has not been in the stomach long enough for acid to digest it. Mallory-Weiss tear with forceful recurrent retching. In a newborn, ask about cracked or bleeding maternal nipples (swallowed blood from breastfeeding).
Coffee grounds (black flecks)Bleed from the stomach (stomach ulcer / PUD)
Bilious (dark green)Obstruction below the entrance of the common bile duct (ampulla of Vater, in the duodenum). Obstruction higher than that will not give bilious emesis. Never normal in a newborn or young child.
Projectile (forceful, recurrent)Obstruction downstream. In the first couple of months of life, think pyloric stenosis; rarely small bowel atresia.
Absence of red flags is not reassuranceA child without bloody, coffee-ground, bilious or projectile emesis is not automatically benign. Things can progress, so keep a low threshold to recheck children who are not improving.

Differential diagnosis by emesis type

BiliousNon-bilious
Intestinal malrotation (with or without volvulus)
Duodenal atresia
NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis)
EMERGENT evaluation		GER (reflux)
Pyloric stenosis
Formula intolerance (e.g. milk protein intolerance)
Duodenal atresia (if the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct)
Gastroenteritis
Malrotation (if the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct)
  • Bilious emesis, suspected pyloric stenosis and malrotation are all emergent evaluations.

Pertinent history for a vomiting child

  • Age (newborn, infant, child, teen): this narrows the differential more than anything else.
  • Nature and timing of emesis: after feeds? recurrent? forceful/projectile? non-bloody non-bilious (NBNB) or bloody/bilious?
  • Associated symptoms: fever, cough, runny nose, wheezing, choking, diarrhea; abdominal pain (arching, drawing legs up); trouble feeding; weight gain or loss; sick contacts, daycare, new foods, travel or animal exposures.
  • Do not assume every vomiting child is reflux or gastroenteritis, even though those are the most common.

2. The Mouth and Ankyloglossia (Tongue-Tie)

Feeding physiology

  • Pediatrics focuses on breastfeeding and latching from birth. Non-nutritive sucking begins as early as 18 weeks gestation; nutritive sucking around 32 weeks.
  • Requires coordination of the tongue, hyoid, mandible and lower lip. The more premature the infant, the less force and coordination, so ineffective breastfeeding is more common; it can still occur in early term (37 weeks) through full term infants.
Oral cavity schematic (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Ankyloglossia

  • Limited tongue mobility due to a restrictive lingual frenulum. Definition is not standardized, and opinions vary on clinical significance and management. The AAP has issued a policy statement because many infants are being referred for frenotomy (or laser release, or lip-tie release) that may not be needed.
  • Prevalence: <1–10% (many have a tie without any dysfunction, so it is under-recorded).

Clinical features

  • Difficulty lifting the tongue.
  • Cannot protrude the tongue past the lower central incisors (in a baby: past the lower gum line).
  • Heart-shaped tongue (notch in the center) when protruded.
  • Difficulty placing the examiner's (gloved) finger between the underside of the tongue and the mandibular alveolus.
Ankyloglossia (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Why it matters

  • Breastfeeding difficulty: painful latch for mom (cuts, scrapes, infection of the breast) and inefficient suckling with poor milk transfer → poor weight gain.
  • Articulation problems later (lingual sounds: t, d, z, s, th, n, l). It is not associated with delayed onset of speech.

Management (stepwise)

  1. Newborn with concerns: refer to a lactation specialist first (family, mom and baby work on efficient, pain-free feeding with adequate growth).
  2. If not improving, baby losing weight, or feeding is very painful and mom wants to keep breastfeeding: frenotomy (definitive treatment).
  3. Later, with articulation difficulty: refer to speech therapy evaluation first; if no improvement, frenotomy is again indicated.
  • Frenotomy: quick snip of the frenulum with surgical scissors, using a grooved spoon-like device to lift the tongue. Often done in the pediatric office without anesthesia, minimal bleeding, and baby feeds right after. Also commonly done at the dentist.

3. Esophageal Atresia and Tracheoesophageal Fistula

  • Congenitally interrupted esophagus. Five types (A–E). Know that type C is the most common (85%).
Types of esophageal atresia / TEF (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
TypeAnatomyFrequency
AEsophageal atresia without TEF: two blind pouches, no connection to the trachea~10%
BAtresia with TEF to the proximal segment<1%
CProximal blind pouch + TEF from the distal esophagus (stomach side) to the trachea~85%
DAtresia with TEF to both proximal and distal segments<1%
EH-type: TEF without atresia (esophagus is continuous, but communicates with the trachea)~4%

Presentation (first days of life)

  • Varies with type; most common is type C.
  • Vomiting (blind upper pouch, cannot pass feeds) and respiratory distress with a fistula: with a proximal fistula, feeds enter the trachea; with a distal fistula, stomach acid travels up into the trachea.

When to suspect it

  • Prenatal ultrasound (~20 weeks): polyhydramnios and/or a small or non-visualized stomach. The baby cannot swallow amniotic fluid, so fluid accumulates and the stomach stays empty.
  • After birth: an NG/OG tube will not pass into the stomach; it coils in the proximal esophagus on x-ray. A tube that threads into the trachea causes coughing.
NG tube coiled in the proximal esophagus (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Treatment

  • Ligation of the fistula (so food and acid stop reaching the lungs) and primary anastomosis of the esophageal segments whenever possible.

Associated anomalies

  • 50% have another congenital anomaly; 25% cardiac.
  • VACTERL association: Vertebral, Anal atresia, Cardiac (PDA, ASD, VSD), TracheoEsophageal fistula, Renal (e.g. urethral atresia with hydronephrosis), Limb (humeral hypoplasia, radial aplasia, hexadactyly, proximally placed thumb).
  • Exam pearl: a two-vessel umbilical cord (single umbilical artery) is commonly associated with VACTERL.
VACTERL association (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

4. Gastroesophageal Reflux (GER) vs Reflux Disease (GERD)

GER: the "happy spitter-upper"

  • Very common in the first 6 months. A normal physiologic process in healthy infants; episodes are brief and cause no symptoms or esophageal injury. Often worsens before it improves. Most outgrow it by 18 months.
  • Infant criteria (3 weeks–12 months): regurgitates >2 times/day for ≥3 weeks without red flags.
  • Typical picture: spit-up 15–20 minutes after a feed, not forceful, milk-colored or curdled, and the baby is happy and playful.
  • Why infants reflux: loose lower esophageal sphincter, lots of time lying flat, and overfeeding (stomach can only hold so much).
GER management = reassurance and reflux precautionsReassure; smaller, more frequent feeds (especially bottle-fed, who are often fed more than the stomach holds); keep upright after feeds (15–20 min in the cases; 20–30 min on the slides) so gravity helps; rarely thicken formula or breast milk.

GERD: when reflux causes complications

  • Reflux episodes associated with esophagitis and poor weight gain (the GERD red flags).
SystemRed flags
SystemicFailure to thrive, feeding refusal / crying with every feed, dystonic neck posturing, dental erosions, anemia
RespiratoryWheezing, stridor, cough, hoarseness, recurrent aspiration pneumonia
GIEsophagitis, esophageal stricture (long term), hematemesis, dysphagia
  • Treatment: supportive measures plus acid suppression: H2 blocker (famotidine) first, then a PPI (omeprazole, etc.) if not improving, as a 4–8 week trial. If still persisting, refer to GI.

Reflux and cough

  • GER can cause cough via an esophageal-bronchial reflex and micro-aspiration irritating the lower respiratory tract. In an older child where it is unclear (they may lack typical GI symptoms), a 24-hour pH monitoring probe can correlate cough with reflux, though this is rarely needed.

5. Pyloric Stenosis

  • Thickening and lengthening of the pylorus: hypertrophy of the circular and longitudinal muscle (muscularis propria) causing gastric outlet obstruction. About 1 in 600 live births; one of the most common GI abnormalities of the newborn.
  • Male : female 3–4 : 1; firstborn males most at risk. Associated with Turner syndrome, trisomy 18 (Edwards) and esophageal atresia.
  • Age 3 weeks to 2 months (<12 weeks; much less likely after). The pyloric muscle is normal at birth and thickens and narrows over time, hence the later presentation.

Presentation

  • Recurrent, projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Baby is hungry, ravenous, feeds again right away, then vomits again. Visible peristaltic waves in a thin baby.
  • Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (loss of HCl from vomiting). The hypokalemia shows up only if vomiting has gone on >3 weeks (delayed presentation).

Diagnosis

  • Palpable "olive" in the upper abdomen = pathognomonic, but rarely found in practice.
  • Pyloric ultrasound is the diagnostic test: pyloric length ≥18 mm and wall thickness >4 mm.
Pyloric ultrasound: longitudinal and transverse views (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Treatment

  • Surgical repair, but first correct dehydration and alkalosis.
  • Rehydrate with normal saline (it has chloride); add potassium only once the patient is voiding.
  • Outpatient pearl: a well-appearing infant with intermittently projectile vomiting who is not growing perfectly may get an outpatient pyloric ultrasound; if positive, admit for surgical repair.

6. Duodenal Atresia

  • Accounts for >50% of congenital intestinal atresias; often associated with trisomy 21.
  • Prenatal: ultrasound (~20 weeks) shows polyhydramnios and a dilated stomach (baby swallows fluid that cannot pass the blind duodenum). Contrast with esophageal atresia, where the stomach is small or absent.
  • Obstruction is often below the ampulla of Vater, so bilious vomiting on day 1 of life.
  • Imaging: abdominal x-ray (KUB) shows the double bubble sign: dilated stomach plus dilated proximal duodenum, with no air below.
  • Treatment: emergent surgical repair.
Duodenal atresia: double bubble (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Timing is the clueDuodenal atresia presents in the newborn period (day 1), usually flagged prenatally. A 5-month-old who was fine until yesterday does not have it.

7. Intestinal Malrotation and Midgut Volvulus

Embryology

  • Normal rotation begins in the 5th week: the midgut extrudes through the umbilical cord and returns, rotating counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, completing around the 12th week.
  • Failed rotation can cause pinching/obstruction of the bowel from the last third of the duodenum and beyond, and midgut volvulus: twisting with decreased blood supply to the intestines and obstruction. Surgical emergency.
Normal rotation vs malrotation (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Epidemiology and presentation

  • Symptomatic neonates: ~1 in 6000 live births. Most present in the first year, but 25–50% are asymptomatic (may never have a volvulus, or present later at any age).
  • Bilious emesis (twisting at the end of the duodenum, below the ampulla).
  • Recurrent abdominal pain (intermittent volvulus: twisting and untwisting).
  • Any age can present with acute obstruction from a developed volvulus: ill-appearing, distended, tender abdomen, bilious emesis.

Diagnosis and treatment

  • Upper GI series (with small bowel follow-through): bird's beak appearance of the duodenum, possibly a corkscrew pattern of contrast. Ultrasound is increasingly used to assess the volvulus and blood flow.
  • Often associated with other congenital defects: congenital diaphragmatic hernia, CHD (heterotaxy), omphalocele, gastroschisis.
  • Treatment: emergent surgical repair.
Bird's beak and corkscrew on upper GI series (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

8. Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele vs Gastroschisis

OmphaloceleGastroschisis
DefectHerniation of bowel into the umbilical cord (failure of the gut to return to the abdomen)Abdominal wall defect, usually to the right of the umbilical cord (not through it)
CoveringCovered by peritoneum (sac), no overlying skinNo covering sac
ContentsBowel; liver may be includedAlways small intestine; other organs sometimes
MalrotationAlwaysAlways
Chromosomal~30% have chromosomal abnormalitiesNot emphasized
Incidence~1 in 5,000 (liver included: ~1 in 10,000)Not given
TreatmentMoist, sterile dressings; surgery once the abdominal cavity can accommodate the bowelSurgical repair ASAP; a silo keeps the bowel moist and protected while the abdomen slowly accommodates it (especially in premature babies)
PrognosisIsolated omphalocele: >90% survivalNot given

9. Clinical Cases: The Approach (Happy Spitter vs Green Vomiter)

How to use these casesThe cases themselves are not what gets tested; the principles are. For each, focus on which features point toward or away from each diagnosis.

Case 1: the "happy spitter-upper" (2-month-old)

  • Story: 2-month-old with spit-up when lying flat and after feeds for a couple of weeks, slowly worsening. Formula/bottle taking 5–6 oz per feed, milk-colored, non-projectile, some back arching but not consistent, morning congestion, mustard-yellow stools, no diarrhea, no fever, 2-month vaccines done, born at 38 weeks with no NICU stay.
  • Exam: afebrile, well-appearing, normal vitals, clear lungs, soft non-distended non-tender abdomen, normal bowel sounds, normal frenulum, anterior fontanelle open, soft and flat.
  • Growth: tracking normally on weight, length and head circumference (no falling percentiles).
Case 1 growth charts (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Case 1 differential: why each is in or out

DiagnosisVerdict and reasoning
TEFUnlikely. No cough or choking with feeds, no recurrent (aspiration) pneumonias, clear lungs; at 2 months a blind-pouch baby would have been diagnosed at birth because they could not feed or grow.
GERMost likely. Age (reflux picks up after ~3 weeks and worsens before it improves); large-volume bottle feeds with a loose LES; time spent lying down; back arching and spit-up after feeds; growing well; normal exam apart from mild congestion (common in reflux).
GERDNot yet. Not causing dysfunction: growing, happy and comfortable. It becomes GERD with pain, back arching, crying when laid flat, poor feeding, poor growth. Educate parents what to watch for.
MalrotationUnlikely: non-bilious, happy and growing, no abdominal pain. A malrotation/volvulus baby would look sick with pain, distension, tenderness and bilious vomiting. Parents should return for bilious, bloody, coffee-ground or forceful recurrent vomiting.
Pyloric stenosisUnlikely: normal exam, non-projectile, well-appearing. Reassess if it becomes recurrent, forceful/projectile, with a ravenous baby who feeds and vomits again; if concern and well-appearing, get an abdominal ultrasound; if positive, admit for surgery.

Case 1 management principles

  • GER: education and reflux precautions (smaller or more frequent feeds, upright 15–20 minutes after feeds).
  • If it becomes GERD (poor growth, fussiness/discomfort with feeds, poor feeding): famotidine first; if not improving, a PPI for a 4–8 week trial; if still persisting, GI referral.

Case 2: the "green vomiter" (5-month-old)

  • Story: 5-month-old with 24 hours of vomiting that is now green-tinged, fussy, bigger belly, cries and vomits with every feed. Previously only milk-colored reflux that resolved after famotidine. No diarrhea, no blood, no respiratory symptoms, no sick contacts at home (she does attend daycare), vaccines up to date, full term, growth tracking at the 50th percentile.
  • Exam: T 99.0°F, HR 130 (mildly tachycardic), ill-appearing but not toxic, moist mucous membranes, clear lungs, distended, diffusely tender abdomen, and an episode of bilious emesis during the visit.

Case 2 differential: why each is in or out

DiagnosisVerdict and reasoning
Pyloric stenosisUnlikely: too old (>12 weeks) and bilious (PS is non-bilious, projectile, ~2–12 weeks; a prolonged course gives hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis).
GERDUnlikely: GERD is not bilious; this is acute, and her prior reflux had resolved (off famotidine).
Malrotation (with volvulus)Most likely: acute onset, recurrent bilious emesis, distension and abdominal pain. She may have had asymptomatic malrotation until a volvulus developed. Emergent evaluation: send straight to the ED (or call 911 if unstable), upper GI series, and transfer to a center with a surgical team; surgical repair if volvulus (decreased blood supply; delay risks catastrophic bowel damage).
Duodenal atresiaUnlikely: bilious, but presents in the newborn period (day 1) and is usually diagnosed prenatally (polyhydramnios, double bubble); she would not have done well at home for 5 months.
GastroenteritisUnlikely: usually acute non-bilious emesis plus diarrhea, with sick contacts. Self-limited; treat with supportive care: smaller, more frequent feeds or small sips, gradually advance diet, ondansetron (Zofran) in the office if at risk for dehydration or not tolerating any PO. Parents can allow no solids as long as the child is drinking and voiding about 3 times per 24 h.
Post-gastroenteritis pearlAfter viral gastroenteritis there is a temporary relative lactase deficiency (enzyme lost from the damaged lining) for about two weeks; milk can cause vomiting again. Use lactose-free or dairy-light products for ~2 weeks.

Principles from both cases

  • Age + character of emesis + growth + exam appearance sort most of these diagnoses.
  • Bilious emesis in a child who looks sick = emergency until malrotation/volvulus is excluded.
  • Happy, growing, non-bilious, normal exam = GER: reassure and educate on red flags to return for.
  • Even a well-appearing baby with a worrying history gets rechecked or imaged (low threshold).
